items_missed: Agenda statement given but never confirmed. 'I'm gonna start with a few questions to get us on the right track and then that would take about maybe like five to six minutes and then I'd be able to build you an accurate [quote]' is a good roadmap with a real timeframe — and then no 'sound good?', no pause for agreement.
Never asked how she was doing. Defensible given she opened with a complaint, but the warm-up never happened in any form.

Additional rooms never asked. Zero questions about a garage, attic, shed, patio, or storage on a customer moving out of a roughly 3,000 square foot rental house into a 2,500 square foot home. She listed items from memory and he took the list as complete — on a house that size, a garage alone can be an hour.
Special considerations never probed — no long walks, narrow hallways, tight turns, low branches — at either address, including a split-level destination.

Packing needs never asked or offered. Not once. She mentioned 'a box or two or bag or two put in the linens in. Maybe, maybe not might just move those myself' and that was the entire conversation about boxes on a whole-house move.
No box count.
Storage stops and additional stops never asked.

Access concerns never asked. No driveway, no parking, no truck staging at either house, and no question about whether the new house's brand-new floors need protection arranged in advance — which is the thing she is most afraid of.
No 'pricing is super simple' opener — 'So basically, we charge by the hour.'
Packing service pricing never given, downstream of never asking.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. This is the most expensive single miss across all eight calls this week. The customer's opening sentence was 'I need some movers but I want to tell you that I had a really bad experience with my last movers,' followed by 'they really messed up a, a lot of my furniture and also the flooring at the rental [house] I was moving into which clearly am responsible for. So I have a claim[] with them.' She is a customer with an open damage claim against another mover, calling specifically about damage risk, and the words 'up to two thousand dollars to repair, replace, or reimburse' were never said. Neither was the 60c-per-pound industry baseline, which is precisely what she is discovering the hard way with her current claim.

Meet Your Mover never mentioned — on a customer who said in plain words 'I just want somebody I can trust that we'll do a good job.' The pre-move email with the mover's photo and name is the literal product answer to that sentence.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned.

No sense-check in the pricing or clock block. It ran roughly 250 words uninterrupted with no 'does that make sense?' — the customer's next move was to change the subject to her own worry ('let me ask you this. The furniture is heavy, will two people be able to do it?'), which is what happens when a monologue ends without a check-in.

No typical time range for a home this size. He went straight to 'I estimate that this move would take anywhere from six to seven hours' with no anchor, so she has no way to tell whether her move is normal, easy, or hard, and no basis to judge the number.
Walk distance never asked or factored at either address.
Traffic never mentioned.
No equivalents or plain-language anchors used.

Save Your Ass speech entirely absent — 0/10. And this was a customer who would have received it better than most: point-nine miles between the two houses, roughly three rooms of furniture, and a woman who has already done this move once in the other direction within the last month. 'You're a mile away — anything small you can shuttle yourself before we get there comes straight off the clock' is both money in her pocket and a way to reduce the number of her things in strangers' hands, which is what she actually cares about.

No deposit never mentioned — and he booked the move without it. She said yes anyway, but the differentiator that makes booking feel risk-free went unused on a customer whose last experience with a moving company ended in a claim. It is also the reassurance that would have covered the open question on the call: if the bed photo comes back and the job needs a third mover at $333/hr, she has already committed with nothing explaining that she can still change or cancel freely.

No BOLDED-list framing and no 'reply with any corrections' verification ask. 'I'm gonna send you an email confirming your move. You can reply back to that email' was said in the context of sending a photo of the bed, not verifying the booking details. On a booking made in the last ninety seconds of a twelve-minute call — date, window, rate, transportation fee, mover count all still fluid — a read-and-confirm ask was the control that mattered.
'Any other questions before I let you go?' never asked. 'If you have any questions, feel free to give us a callback' is a standing offer at the door, not an invitation to raise something now.
Hours and how to reach us never given.

Customer's name used zero times. He collected it ('Melissa, [Juarez]') and then never said it again in twelve minutes — on the one call this week where using a distressed customer's name repeatedly would have done the most work.

The photo follow-up has no owner and no channel. She offered ('this is my cell so if you want to text me where to send that I'll get it to you tonight') and he answered 'Yes please' and then redirected to email without ever texting her, confirming a number, or setting a deadline. The third-mover decision — a $111/hour swing — now hangs on an unassigned follow-up.
top_strength: Jules did the hardest thing on this call correctly and he did it in the first ten seconds. A customer opened by telling him she'd been burned, and instead of pivoting to a pitch or getting defensive on the industry's behalf, he opened the door wider: 'Oh, no. Tell me about it.' Then he stayed in it — 'I'm so sorry that happened in your last move. When was your last move?' — and let her tell the whole story: the damaged furniture, the damaged rental flooring she is now personally liable for, the open claim, the recommendation she trusted that turned out badly, and the real fear underneath it all, which is not about this move but about the house she just finished remodeling ('not only does my stuff get back home without getting further damage but they didn't, don't mess up my brand-new. Floors in my house as well'). That is a rep who let a customer finish, and it is why a call that opened on a complaint closed on a booking. He then did something concrete about it rather than just sympathizing. Unprompted, inside the what's-included list, he described exactly the protection she was afraid of going without: 'for the house, for both houses. If we're gonna lay out kind of like floor runners on the floor so we can protect that as well and we also put coverings on doors and wall corners and all that to protect the house as well.' Floor runners and corner guards, volunteered before she asked, against a customer whose specific nightmare is scratched floors — that is the right instinct even though he never connected it back to her story out loud. His handling of the heavy-furniture objection was equally good. She asked 'the furniture is heavy, will two people be able to do it?' and instead of reassuring her blindly he qualified it with a usable threshold — 'How heavy are we talking about? Do you think any of those way more than 300 pounds on its own?' — then, when she described a dropped adjustable bed from her last move, he offered the professional answer she hadn't gotten before ('for the bed if needed we're gonna take it apart instead of move it'), asked for a photo so he could verify capability rather than guess, and priced the contingency transparently on the spot: 'if anything if we need three guys the hours rate basically is $111 per hour per mover. So for three guys it's gonna be $333.' Per mover per hour, stated correctly, with the upgrade path priced before she had to ask what it would cost. His probe on stairs was also the most precise of the week — he caught 'mostly a one story. The master bedroom is the only thing up a flight of stairs' at origin and the split-level with six stairs at destination, which is exactly the detail that separates a real estimate from a guess.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix, and it is a big one: Jules had the most differentiator-ready customer any Einstein rep will get this quarter and played zero of them. Read her own words back — 'they really messed up a lot of my furniture and also the flooring,' 'I have a claim with them,' 'I just want somebody I can trust.' That is a customer describing, in order, No Worries Damage Coverage and Meet Your Mover, and neither was mentioned. The response she needed, right after 'I'm so sorry that happened': 'Two things about how we handle exactly that. First, every move carries our No Worries Damage Coverage — up to two thousand dollars to repair, replace, or reimburse accidental damage, and that covers the doors, floors and walls at both houses, not just what's in the truck. Most movers give you sixty cents a pound, which is why your claim is going the way it's going. Second, a few days before the nineteenth I'll email you a photo and a short bio of the actual two guys coming to your house, so you know who's walking onto those new floors before they get there. And we give you an arrival window with an on-time guarantee — if we miss it we start discounting.' That is under a minute, it is three rubric bullets worth ten points, and more importantly it is the only part of this call that speaks to the reason she picked up the phone. He had the right empathy and no product behind it. Estimate-accuracy flag, and this one goes in the bottom-4 file: he quoted six to seven hours and $1,629 for roughly three rooms of furniture moving point-nine miles, with no boxes, no packing, mostly single-story at origin and six stairs at destination — and he never stated a typical range for the home size to justify it. Count what she actually listed: a king adjustable bed, a queen bed, two nightstands, two dressers, two TVs, a sofa, a love seat, a small love seat, an armchair, an L-desk that comes apart, an office chair, a fridge, a washer/dryer combo, two stools. That is roughly twenty items over a mile, and she told him so up front — 'it's really three rooms, not even three full rooms of furniture and it's a point nine mile drive.' Seven hours on that inventory is the large-home conservative pad the estimate-accuracy work is chasing: the square footage was 3,000 and 2,500 and the number appears to have been priced off the house rather than off the list. He should have said the range out loud and shown his work — 'a house this size normally runs X to Y, but you're only moving three rooms a mile down the road, so I'd put you at four to five' — because he cannot be corrected on reasoning he never voiced, and if this one comes in at four and a half hours it will read as a win when it was actually a 40% miss. Worth pulling the actual on this one; it booked for the 19th. Second priority: he booked the move and skipped the entire close. No deposit, no bolded-details email framing, no 'reply with any corrections,' no 'any other questions before I let you go?', no hours. He committed a nervous customer to a date in the last ninety seconds of the call with an unresolved third-mover question, an unpriced possible upgrade from $222 to $333 an hour, and a bed photo that has no delivery channel and no deadline. At minimum: 'You're on for the nineteenth, eight-thirty to nine. There's no deposit and nothing on a card, so if anything changes you just tell me. I'm texting you now so you have my number for the bed photo — send it tonight and I'll confirm by tomorrow whether two guys or three. The confirmation email has the date, window, rate and the seventy-five dollar transportation fee bolded at the top; give those a read and reply if anything's off.' Third, use her name. Twelve minutes with an upset customer and 'Melissa' was never said once.
phone_presence_notes: Real empathy delivered at the right moment — 'Oh, no. Tell me about it,' 'I'm so sorry that happened in your last move,' and 'we're gonna do our best to make sure this move would go as smoothly as possible' turned a customer who opened on a grievance into one who booked and closed with 'thank you so much' — held back only by never using her name across twelve minutes and by letting the 'I just want somebody I can trust' line pass without a direct answer.
